title: One command over orderflow
intro: Install Graphify, point it at a fifteen-file monorepo, and watch a queryable map fall out of it. Then the part nobody puts in the demo: check whether it was worth doing.

provenance.source: a replayed session over labs/sample-project. The run log follows the shape documented in labs/M04-graphify-end-to-end/README.md; the node, edge, caller and community figures are reproducible with labs/shared_tools/kg_extract.py and checkable by hand against labs/sample-project/README.md. Steps 3, 4, 5 and 6 carry their own citations.

foot: Reproduce every step in labs/M04-graphify-end-to-end/README.md · the four-arm measured version is Capstone 2

steps.title: Install once, register the skill
narrative: Two commands. The first puts the graphify binary on your PATH; the second is the one people skip and then wonder why /graphify does nothing in their assistant.

graphify install writes the skill registration for every AI assistant it finds on the machine — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI. Nothing is deployed and no key is asked for, because the code pass never calls a model.
steps.youDo: Run uv tool install graphifyy && graphify install. If graphify: command not found follows, your uv or pipx bin directory is not on PATH — that is the entire failure mode.

terminal.text: uv tool install graphifyy && graphify install
Tip: set MOONSHOT_API_KEY to use Kimi K2.6 for semantic extraction — 3x cheaper, richer graphs.

steps.title: Point it at orderflow
narrative: orderflow is the course's running example: a B2B order-tracking monorepo with a billing service, an orders service, a notifications worker and three shared modules. Fifteen files, deliberately small enough that you can verify every edge by hand.
One command from the project root. No configuration file, no schema to declare, no index to warm up. Read the log closely — three of its lines encode design decisions rather than status.
steps.youDo: cd labs/sample-project then graphify update . — or type /graphify . inside your assistant, which runs the same pass.
steps.claudeSays: With the skill registered, the assistant shells out to the same binary and then reads graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md instead of opening your source files.

terminal.text: Re-extracting code files in . (no LLM needed)...
[graphify watch] graph.json, graph.html and GRAPH_REPORT.md updated in graphify-out
Code graph updated. For doc/paper/image changes run /graphify --update in your AI assistant.

cells: the machine layer · M09's MCP server loads this
so re-runs only touch changed files

steps.title: 36 nodes, 22 edges — and which ones are guesses
narrative: Open graph.json and count. Thirty-six nodes: fourteen modules, eighteen functions, four classes. Twenty-two edges between them.

The number that matters is the split on the right. Nine edges are EXTRACTED — read straight off the syntax tree, 100% confidence. Thirteen are INFERRED — a heuristic matched a bare name to a definition and attached a confidence score. Graphify is the tool in this space that tells you which of its answers are facts and which are guesses, and on a repo this small you can audit every one.
steps.youDo: Offline route, same numbers: python labs/shared_tools/kg_extract.py labs/sample-project --out graph.json. It prints the node-kind and provenance breakdowns you see here.

items.label: EXTRACTED
items.note: off the AST · 100% confidence · zero hallucination risk

items.label: INFERRED
items.note: bare-name resolution · carries a confidence score · audit these

steps.title: It rediscovers the architecture doc
narrative: Leiden clustering runs on every build. On orderflow the 36 nodes fall into three communities that line up with billing, orders and notifications — the exact subsystem split docs/architecture.md claims, recovered from call edges alone with no doc in sight.

It also flags one god node: shared/db.py. Every service imports it, so it bridges all three clusters. That is not a bug report. It is a blast-radius warning — a change there touches more of the repo than a change anywhere else.
steps.youDo: Open graphify-out/graph.html, find the three colored clusters, then read GRAPH_REPORT.md and check it names the same three. If the two disagree, you have found M11's desync problem four modules early.

before.title: WHAT THE GRAPH FOUND, WITHOUT READING DOCS

after.title: WHAT THAT DOES AND DOESN'T MEAN

view.text: Communities are a hypothesis about your architecture, not a verdict on it. On orderflow they match the doc because orderflow is clean. On a legacy monolith the clusters will cut across your stated module boundaries — and that disagreement is the finding, not an error in the tool.

steps.title: Ask it a caller question
narrative: Artifacts on disk are potential energy. The kinetic form is a query. Ask the thing an agent asks constantly: who calls this?

The answer comes back as a small structured object — the symbol, its kind, where it lives, its callers, its callees, its transitive blast radius, and whether the name was ambiguous. Compare that to the alternative: grep decode_jwt, open every hit, read enough of each file to tell a real call site from a mention in a docstring.
steps.youDo: graphify query "What components depend on DatabasePool?" and graphify path "post_invoice" "decode_jwt". Check both answers against the ground-truth list at the bottom of labs/sample-project/README.md — at fifteen files you genuinely can.
steps.claudeSays: The assistant fetches the matching nodes and edges and reasons over those. shared/auth.py never enters the context window.

One direct caller: verify_token, same file. That is the route every

decode_jwt. Blast radius 2, and the name is unambiguous, so this is

steps.title: The part the demo leaves out
narrative: orderflow is fifteen files. It is far below the roughly 500-file line where graph tooling starts paying for itself, and the honest read of this whole walkthrough is that on this repo the graph is a teaching aid, not a saving.

Here is that claim measured rather than asserted. Capstone 2 ran the same four-arm campaign on a 36-file Spring Boot service: 48 fresh sessions, medians of three per cell. Every graph configuration lost. The best arm was one 55-line root CLAUDE.md.

So take the mechanics from this module and hold the multiple loosely. The vendor's 71.5x came from a 52-file corpus with a favourable query; independent replications land between 6.8x and 49x; below the floor you go backwards. Measure your own repo before you commit to a pipeline.
steps.youDo: Ask your assistant one structural question about orderflow with and without /graphify ., and write down both token counts. That number is yours, and you reuse it in the capstone.

state.label: measured · priorauth-api-boot3 · 36 files · 4 questions, medians of 3

before.title: BELOW THE FLOOR, THE GRAPH LOSES

after.title: WHY IT GOES THAT WAY AT 36 FILES

view.text: At this size grep answers a caller question in two turns, so there is barely anything for the graph to beat — while the graph is small, half its edges are AMBIGUOUS, and forced edge-walking burned 17 to 18 turns on the comprehension questions. Which lever wins is a property of the repo and the question mix, not of the tool. Same campaign on spring-framework's 9,195 files flips the answer.
